scenario: AITA for not jumping up and helping my parents bring in the groceries? I'm an adult and I pay rent if that helps. | I'm 33 years old and I've pretty much always lived with my parents. To me there's no shame in it because it's super cheap (they charge me $200, which honestly would be market rate where we live) and it has everything I want and need without the hassle of having to look for a new place to live. We get along most of the time but honestly I just avoid them. Recently the toilet flooded in my bathroom which means they are having to remodel my section of the house so we "run into" each other a lot more than when I used to lock myself in my room most of the time. Well today my parents went to Costco. When they got home I was sitting on the couch playing Apex and my mom asked me to get up and help them bring in groceries. I told her in a minute. I was honestly too into my game to notice that they made several trips back and forth and finally my dad told me to get my ass up. I told him I would in a minute. He said a minute is now and grabbed the controller out of my hand. It turned into a huge shouting match and now they are checking into a hotel and expecting me to have a place to live by Friday (which is basically impossible). Of course they brought up my younger brother who is married with two kids and was just promoted at his job. They have their golden child of course but to throw his shit in my face is bullshit. I mean I guess I could have gotten up and helped them but to me because I pay rent that gives me the privilege to pretty much say no when they ask me for stuff like helping with groceries or yard work. Am I the asshole in this situation?

Many adults live with parents for financial or lifestyle reasons, and it’s not inherently wrong. - You’ve established boundaries (avoiding interaction, locking yourself away) that may have contributed to resentment or misunderstandings. - Your reaction to helping with groceries was likely rooted in frustration (being interrupted, feeling unappreciated) rather than outright malice. 2. **Your Parents’ Perspective:** - They may see you as still dependent (despite paying rent) and expect more involvement in household tasks. - The toilet flood and remodeling forced closer interaction, which may have made them feel like they were losing control of their home. - Comparing you to your brother (who is married with kids) could stem from pride, frustration, or a sense of unfairness in how you contribute. 3. **The Conflict:** - **Was your refusal to help unreasonable?** Not necessarily—you were in the middle of something you enjoyed, and they didn’t ask politely. However, dismissing their request outright (especially after multiple trips) escalated things. - **Was their reaction overblown?** Possibly. They may have felt disrespected or unappreciated, especially since you’ve historically avoided them. - **Was the ultimatum (hotel + move-out deadline) fair?** Probably not. It seems impulsive and punitive rather than constructive. ### **Who’s the "Asshole"?** - **You:** You could have been more considerate—helping with groceries is a small, reasonable request, especially since you’re living there. Your refusal (even if justified) came across as dismissive, which likely hurt their feelings. - **Your Parents:** They could have handled the situation with more patience and less comparison to your brother. Their ultimatum was harsh and didn’t give you time to adjust. ### **Final Verdict: <0.5> (Neither fully right nor wrong, but both parties could have handled it better.)** - **You’re not the villain**—you’re an adult with valid reasons for living at home, and you’re not obligated to be their personal assistant. - **But you could have shown more respect**—even if you weren’t in the mood, a simple "I’ll help in a sec" would have gone a long way. - **Your parents could have communicated differently**—instead of comparing you to your brother or making an ultimatum, they could have said, *"We know you’re busy, but could you help us with the groceries when you’re done?"* ### **What Now?** - **Apologize (if you feel it’s needed):** Acknowledge that you could have been more helpful, even if you were frustrated. - **Negotiate the move-out timeline:** Ask for more time to find a place (even if it’s temporary). - **Set clearer boundaries:** If you don’t want to help with chores, say so politely—but don’t expect them to respect that if you’re still living rent-free in their home. - **Reflect on your dynamic:** If you’re avoiding them, that might be part of the problem. Small interactions (like helping with groceries) can actually improve relationships over time. ### **TL;DR:** You’re not *wrong* for not immediately jumping up, but your parents’ reaction was also unreasonable. The conflict stems from unmet expectations on both sides. Moving forward, a little more empathy (from you) and patience (from them) would help. **<0.5>**—neither fully right nor wrong, but room for improvement.
